spans: The universe exists for over 9 billion years before our planet forms.
Molten, bombarded young Earth. Named after Hades. Oceans may already exist by 4.4 billion years ago.
First life appears. No oxygen in the air; the sky was likely hazy and orange-tinted.
Oxygen arrives, complex cells evolve, and Earth freezes over at least twice.
The eon of visible life: animals, plants, dinosaurs, mammals and us.
Oldest known rocks on Earth date from this era.
Stromatolites built by microbes grow in shallow seas.
Early continents and possibly the first supercontinent.
The Great Oxidation Event changes the planet's chemistry forever.
Sometimes called the 'Boring Billion', but sex and multicellular algae appear.
Snowball Earth, then the first large animals.
Old life: trilobites, fish, first forests, amphibians and reptiles.
The age of reptiles and dinosaurs.
Supercontinent Rodinia begins to break apart.
Ice reaches the equator: Snowball Earth.
First large, complex organisms, many unlike anything alive today.
Explosion of animal body plans; eyes, shells and predators appear.
Seas full of trilobites and nautiloids; first land plants.
Jawed fish and the first plants with vascular tissue.
The age of fishes. First forests and first four-legged animals.
Coal swamps and giant insects in oxygen-rich air.
Supercontinent Pangaea; ends in the worst mass extinction ever.
Life recovers; first dinosaurs and first mammals.
Flowering plants, T. rex, and an asteroid at the end.
Mammals diversify; early whales, horses and primates.
Grasslands spread; apes, and the human line splits from chimpanzees.
Ice ages and the genus Homo.
A hot world; palm trees near the poles.
Apes thrive across Africa and Eurasia.
Ice ages, mammoths, Neanderthals and early modern humans.
Warm and stable climate: farming, cities, writing and everything after.
The Old Stone Age, over 99% of human technological history.
Farming, villages and pottery. Dates vary widely by region.
First metalworking. Otzi the Iceman carried a copper axe.
Bronze tools, writing, and the first states. Ends in a collapse.
Cheaper, stronger iron spreads across Eurasia.
Greece, Rome, Persia, Han China and Maurya India.
From the fall of Rome in the West to the age of print and ocean voyages.
A mild climate in the North Atlantic region helps harvests and population growth.
Colder centuries: frost fairs on the frozen Thames, failed harvests, advancing glaciers.
Global empires, the printing press, science and the Reformation.
Steam, factories and coal transform Britain, then the world.
Industry, nations, world wars, electricity and computers.
The US and USSR face off without fighting each other directly.
The oldest continuous living cultures on Earth: at least 50,000 years, possibly 65,000.
City-states of southern Mesopotamia: Uruk, Ur, Lagash. Inventors of cuneiform writing.
Three thousand years of pharaohs, from Narmer to Cleopatra.
Palace of Knossos, bull-leaping frescoes and the undeciphered Linear A script.
Planned cities like Mohenjo-daro with drains and standard bricks. Script still undeciphered.
Often called the first empire, founded by Sargon of Akkad.
Anatolian power that rivalled Egypt and signed the earliest surviving peace treaty.
The world of Agamemnon and the Trojan War legends.
Bronze ritual vessels and oracle bones, the earliest Chinese writing.
Mesoamerica's early civilization, famous for colossal stone heads.
Longest Chinese dynasty; the age of Confucius and Laozi.
Military superpower of the Near East, capital Nineveh.
Cyrus the Great's empire, from the Aegean to the Indus.
Senate, consuls and conquest of the Mediterranean.
Most of the Indian subcontinent, under Chandragupta and Ashoka.
Silk Road, paper, and the name of China's majority ethnic group.
One of the largest cities in the world in its time, in the Valley of Mexico.
From Augustus to the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus.
Ethiopian trading empire that minted its own coins and adopted Christianity early.
Tikal, Palenque, Copan: astronomy, a full writing system and the Long Count calendar.
A golden age of Indian mathematics, astronomy and art.
The Eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople for over a thousand years.
Cosmopolitan dynasty; its capital Chang'an was one of the world's largest cities.
Stretched from Spain to Central Asia.
Baghdad's House of Wisdom and the Islamic Golden Age.
Norse raiders, traders and settlers from Russia to Newfoundland.
From Athelstan's unification to union with Scotland.
Paper money, movable type and gunpowder weapons.
Neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire, as Voltaire joked.
Stone city of southern Africa at the centre of a gold trade.
Henry II to Richard III: Magna Carta, Parliament, the Black Death and the Wars of the Roses.
The largest contiguous land empire in history.
Home of Mansa Musa and the scholars of Timbuktu.
Six centuries, from Anatolia to Vienna's gates.
Forbidden City, Great Wall rebuilt, and Zheng He's treasure fleets.
Triple Alliance ruled from Tenochtitlan, a city on a lake.
Largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas; ran on roads and knotted-string records (quipu).
Akbar, Shah Jahan and the Taj Mahal.
At its height it ruled about a quarter of the world's land and people.
Federation of six colonies on 1 January 1901.
The first communist state, until its dissolution.
Round arches, thick walls, small windows.
Pointed arches, rib vaults and flying buttresses let walls dissolve into stained glass.
Rebirth of classical learning: perspective, anatomy and humanism.
Drama and movement: Caravaggio, Bernini, Bach.
Emotion, nature and the sublime; Chopin, Turner, Mary Shelley.
Painting light in the open air: Monet, Renoir, Morisot.
Born in New Orleans from blues, ragtime and brass bands.
Electric guitars, youth culture and the teenager.
Born at block parties in the Bronx, New York.
events: The universe begins expanding from an extremely hot, dense state. Space itself, not just matter, starts to stretch.
About 380,000 years after the Big Bang the universe cools enough for atoms to form and light travels freely. We still detect this glow as the cosmic microwave background.
After the cosmic 'dark ages', the first stars form from hydrogen and helium, roughly 100 to 200 million years after the Big Bang (estimate).
The James Webb Space Telescope has spotted galaxies shining about 300 million years after the Big Bang.
A cloud of gas and dust collapses, possibly triggered by a nearby supernova. Leftover material forms the planets.
Oldest solids in the solar system
Calcium-aluminium-rich grains found inside meteorites like Allende are dated to about 4.567 billion years ago.
Our planet assembles from colliding rocks in the young solar system.
A Mars-sized body, nicknamed Theia, likely crashes into the young Earth. Debris forms the Moon.
Zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia are about 4.4 billion years old, and hint that liquid water already existed.
The Acasta Gneiss in Canada's Northwest Territories is about 4 billion years old.
Carbon in 3.7-billion-year-old Greenland rocks may come from living things. Still debated.
Layered structures built by microbial mats in the Pilbara of Western Australia are among the oldest widely accepted evidence of life.
Oxygen made by cyanobacteria builds up in the air for the first time. It poisoned much early life and made rust-red banded iron rocks.
Eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus, appear. One swallowed a bacterium that became the mitochondrion (approximate date).
Bangiomorpha, a red alga from Arctic Canada, is the oldest known organism with sexual reproduction.
The Sturtian glaciation covers the planet in ice, possibly to the equator, for tens of millions of years.
The first large complex organisms, soft quilted forms with no obvious heads or mouths. Named after the Ediacara Hills in South Australia.
Most major animal groups appear in the fossil record within about 20 million years: eyes, legs, shells and the first predators.
A Canadian rock bed preserves soft-bodied oddities such as five-eyed Opabinia and the predator Anomalocaris.
Simple plants related to liverworts begin to colonise bare continents.
Glaciation and falling sea levels wipe out about 85% of marine species.
A fish with wrist-like fins and a neck, a transitional form between fish and four-legged animals.
A series of crises devastates reefs and many fish groups.
The continents merge into one supercontinent surrounded by a single ocean, Panthalassa.
Hylonomus, a small lizard-like animal, lived in hollow tree stumps in Nova Scotia. Amniote eggs free animals from water.
Meganeura, a dragonfly relative with a wingspan around 70 cm, flies through oxygen-rich Carboniferous forests.
The end-Permian extinction, the worst in Earth's history: about 90% of marine species vanish. Massive Siberian volcanism is the prime suspect.
Small, two-legged early dinosaurs such as Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus appear in what is now Argentina.
Small, furry, probably nocturnal mammaliaforms appear alongside early dinosaurs.
Volcanism as the Atlantic opens clears the way for dinosaurs to dominate.
The supercontinent starts splitting; the Atlantic Ocean begins to open.
A feathered dinosaur with teeth and clawed wings, found in Bavaria. Key evidence that birds are dinosaurs.
Angiosperms appear and soon transform landscapes and insect life.
Lives in western North America during the last few million years of the Cretaceous.
Asteroid ends the age of dinosaurs
A 10 km asteroid strikes Chicxulub, Mexico. About three quarters of species die, including all non-avian dinosaurs. Birds survive.
A sudden burst of carbon warms the planet by around 5 to 8 degrees C. Studied today as a natural analogue for climate change.
Small tree-dwelling primates spread across the northern continents.
Pakicetus, a wolf-sized land mammal from Pakistan, is an early relative of whales.
A permanent ice sheet forms on Antarctica as CO2 falls and the Southern Ocean opens.
A skull from Chad, nicknamed Toumai, may be close to the split between the human and chimpanzee lines.
Ardipithecus ramidus from Ethiopia: walked upright on the ground but still climbed with grasping feet.
Footprints preserved in volcanic ash in Tanzania prove upright walking 3.66 million years ago.
Tools from Lomekwi, Kenya, predate the genus Homo.
An Australopithecus afarensis skeleton found in Ethiopia in 1974, named after the Beatles song played at the camp.
A jawbone from Ledi-Geraru, Ethiopia, is the oldest known fossil of our genus.
The Quaternary begins: ice sheets grow and shrink in rhythm with Earth's orbit.
Tall, long-legged humans who soon spread from Africa to Georgia, China and Java.
Acheulean hand axes, teardrop-shaped tools, are made for over a million years with little change.
Burnt bone and plant ash in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, suggest early use of fire.
Sima de los Huesos in Spain holds remains of at least 28 people on the Neanderthal lineage.
Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, push our species back to about 300,000 years.
A crosshatch pattern drawn in ochre on a stone flake in Blombos Cave, South Africa.
Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians cross the sea from Southeast Asia. At least 50,000 years ago; Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land suggests around 65,000.
The main dispersal of modern humans that gives rise to most people living outside Africa today.
Interbreeding leaves most people of non-African descent with around 1 to 2% Neanderthal DNA.
A warty pig painted in a Sulawesi cave, Indonesia, at least 45,500 years ago. A nearby scene was dated to 51,200 years in 2024.
Flutes made of bird bone and mammoth ivory from caves in southern Germany, around 42,000 years old.
The last Neanderthals vanish from Europe, though their genes live on in us.
Lion-Man and Venus of Hohle Fels
Carved ivory figures from Swabian caves in Germany, among the oldest sculptures known.
Lions, rhinos and horses painted in a French cave, sealed by a rockfall and rediscovered in 1994.
Ice sheets reach their greatest extent. Sea level is about 120 m lower; Tasmania and New Guinea are joined to mainland Australia.
Human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, dated to 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, earlier than many expected.
A baboon bone from Congo with notches in groups, possibly one of the oldest counting tools.
Hundreds of painted animals in a French cave, found by teenagers and their dog in 1940.
Wolves become dogs, at least 15,000 years ago and maybe much earlier. The first domesticated animal.
The last ice age ends; a warm, stable climate allows farming to start in several places independently.
Massive carved stone pillars in Turkey built by hunter-gatherers, centuries before farming or pottery.
Wheat, barley and lentils are domesticated in the Fertile Crescent.
One of the oldest walled settlements, with a stone tower over 8 m high.
A Neolithic town in Turkey with no streets: people entered their houses through the roof.
Rice is domesticated along the Yangtze River.
A sudden cold snap, likely from a meltwater lake draining into the North Atlantic.
Wheels appear in Mesopotamia, used first for pottery and then for carts.
The African Humid Period ends and a green Sahara with lakes and hippos turns into desert.
A man is shot with an arrow in the Alps. His body was found by hikers in 1991 with his clothes, copper axe and last meal intact.
Cuneiform in Sumer, used first for accounting. Egyptian hieroglyphs appear around the same time.
Narmer, the first pharaoh, unites Upper and Lower Egypt.
The first circular ditch and bank. The giant sarsen stones are raised around 2500 BCE.
Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium, is found in human remains around 4,900 years old in Sweden.
Completed for the pharaoh Khufu. It was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years.
Builds the first known empire across Mesopotamia.
A long mega-drought, linked to the collapse of Egypt's Old Kingdom and the Akkadian Empire.
A small population survives on Wrangel Island off Siberia until about 4,000 years ago, after the Great Pyramid was built.
Babylonian laws carved on a stone stele: 282 laws, including 'an eye for an eye'.
A huge volcanic eruption on Santorini buries the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri under ash.
The Hurrian Hymn No. 6, written on a clay tablet at Ugarit, Syria.
Sacred hymns of early Hinduism, passed down orally for centuries (approximate date).
Sculpted by Thutmose. Found in his workshop in Amarna in 1912.
The boy pharaoh dies at about 19. His nearly intact tomb is found in 1922.
Egypt and the Hittites fight one of the largest chariot battles ever. Both claim victory.
Egypt's Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III sign a peace treaty. A copy hangs at the UN.
Within decades the Hittites, Mycenaeans and many Levantine cities fall. Causes include drought, earthquakes and raiders called the Sea Peoples.
The traditional date of the first Games at Olympia. The only event was a foot race.
The legendary date when Romulus founds the city.
The kingdom of Lydia in Anatolia strikes coins from electrum, a gold-silver alloy.
His teachings on family, duty and good government shape East Asia for 2,500 years.
Cleisthenes reforms Athens so that citizens vote directly on laws. Women, slaves and foreigners are excluded.
Athenians defeat a Persian army. The marathon race recalls the legend of a runner carrying the news.
Spartans hold the pass at Thermopylae for three days; the Greek fleet then defeats Persia at Salamis.
Siddhartha Gautama teaches in northern India (5th century BCE; exact dates are uncertain).
The temple of Athena in Athens, originally brightly painted.
The 'Father of History' reports that the Neuri people each turn into wolves for a few days every year. He says he doesn't believe it.
An epidemic during the war with Sparta kills perhaps a quarter of Athens, including the statesman Pericles.
Sentenced to death by an Athenian jury, he drinks hemlock.
Dies in Babylon at 32 after conquering an empire from Greece to India.
The geometry textbook used for over 2,000 years.
The Mauryan emperor is so horrified by the bloodshed that he embraces Buddhism and non-violence.
Eratosthenes estimates Earth's circumference using shadows in two Egyptian cities. He was close.
Qin Shi Huang becomes the first emperor, standardising writing, coins and weights and linking early walls.
The Carthaginian general marches an army with war elephants into Italy.
Thousands of life-size clay soldiers are buried with the first emperor. Found by farmers digging a well in 1974.
Rome razes its old rival. The story that the fields were sown with salt is a later invention.
After Zhang Qian's missions west, Han China trades silk with Central Asia and eventually Rome.
A bronze gear-driven device that predicted eclipses and planetary positions, found in a shipwreck. Often called the first analog computer.
Stabbed on the Ides of March (15 March) by senators claiming to save the Republic.
Octavian takes the title Augustus; the Roman Republic becomes an empire.
Includes King Lycaon, turned into a wolf by Zeus for serving him human flesh. Origin of the word 'lycanthropy'.
Executed in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate (around 30 to 33 CE).
Burns for six days in July. Nero blames the Christians. He did not really fiddle, as the fiddle didn't exist yet.
In Petronius's Satyricon, a guest tells of a soldier who strips by the tombs, turns into a wolf, and is wounded in the neck.
Traditionally dated 24 August, though evidence now suggests October. Pliny the Younger wrote an eyewitness account.
Inaugural games last 100 days. It could hold about 50,000 spectators.
Cai Lun reports a papermaking method to the Han emperor.
Construction begins across northern Britain, marking the edge of the Roman Empire.
Probably smallpox, carried back by Roman troops from the east. Kills millions.
Constantine and Licinius grant tolerance to Christians across the Roman Empire.
On 24 August, Alaric's army sacks Rome, the first time in 800 years the city falls to a foreign enemy.
End of the Western Roman Empire
The Germanic general Odoacer deposes the last emperor, the teenage Romulus Augustulus.
The worst year to be alive
A volcanic dust veil dims the sun across Europe and Asia for 18 months. Summers fail and famine follows.
Justinian's great church in Constantinople. Its dome seemed to float on light.
The first known pandemic of bubonic plague devastates the Mediterranean world.
Muhammad receives his first revelation in a cave near Mecca, according to Islamic tradition.
Indian mathematician Brahmagupta writes rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers.
Charles Martel's Franks defeat an Umayyad army in central France.
Norse raiders attack the island monastery in England on 8 June, often counted as the start of the Viking Age.
On Christmas Day, Pope Leo III crowns him emperor of the Romans in St Peter's.
Working at Baghdad's House of Wisdom, he writes the book that gives us the word 'algebra'. 'Algorithm' comes from his name.
The oldest surviving dated printed book, found in a sealed cave at Dunhuang, China.
Leif Erikson reaches 'Vinland'. A Norse site at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland, confirms the story.
Murasaki Shikibu, a lady at the Japanese court, writes what is often called the first novel.
A law code of King Cnut, drafted by Archbishop Wulfstan, warns priests to guard their flock from 'the ravenous werewolf', meaning the devil. One of the oldest uses of the word.
Song China issues official paper notes, called jiaozi, in Sichuan.
Guido of Arezzo develops the staff and the 'ut-re-mi' syllables used to teach singing.
A new star in the sky
Chinese astronomers record a 'guest star' visible in daylight for weeks. Its remains are the Crab Nebula.
The Catholic and Orthodox churches split.
William of Normandy defeats King Harold on 14 October. England's ruling class, language and laws change forever.
William the Conqueror's survey of who owned what in England, down to the pigs.
Often called the oldest university in continuous operation in the Western world.
The First Crusade captures the city on 15 July, followed by a massacre of its inhabitants.
King Henry I of England dies, chroniclers say, after eating 'a surfeit of lampreys' against his doctor's advice.
Abbot Suger's new choir at Saint-Denis near Paris combines pointed arches, rib vaults and huge windows. He wanted church walls to glow with 'divine light'.
German abbess, composer, visionary and scientist. One of the earliest composers whose name and music survive.
Construction lasts nearly two centuries. Its flying buttresses were added as the walls rose higher.
Four knights kill the Archbishop in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December, after Henry II's angry words.
Marie de France writes a lay about a noble werewolf betrayed by his wife. The wolf is the hero; the humans are the monsters.
The Ayyubid sultan retakes the city on 2 October, triggering the Third Crusade.
Gerald of Wales tells of a priest in Ireland who meets a talking wolf. A man and woman of Ossory, cursed to live as wolves for seven years, need the last rites.
After Richard the Lionheart dies from a crossbow wound, his brother John takes the throne. He loses Normandy in 1204.
A French romance, later translated into Middle English, in which a prince turned werewolf protects the hero.
Temujin is proclaimed universal ruler of the Mongols.
Founded by scholars fleeing riots in Oxford after a woman was killed.
Crowds of young people march for the Holy Land. Most never reach it. How much is legend is debated.
Rebel barons force King John to seal the charter at Runnymede on 15 June. The king can no longer simply do as he pleases.
Sets church rules for all of Christendom: yearly confession, and distinctive dress for Jews and Muslims.
John dies of dysentery in October during a civil war; a French prince holds London. Henry III is crowned at 9.
Restores ordinary people's rights in royal forests: grazing pigs, gathering wood, and no death penalty for poaching deer.
Built in only 38 years, unusually fast, so it is almost pure Early English Gothic.
A manuscript of Latin and German songs about drinking, gambling, love and fortune, copied around this time.
Sundiata Keita defeats the Sosso king and founds the Mali Empire.
Mongol armies crush Polish and Hungarian forces at Legnica and Mohi in April, then withdraw after the Great Khan dies.
The monk-chronicler of St Albans records events, drawings, maps and even an elephant given to Henry III.
English law books of the time say an outlaw 'bears a wolf's head': cast outside the law, he could be killed like a wolf.
Florence mints a gold coin that becomes a standard currency of European trade.
A volcano on Lombok, Indonesia, has one of the largest eruptions of the last 10,000 years. Famine hits England; mass graves at Spitalfields in London may date from it.
Barons force Henry III to accept a council and regular parliaments. Issued in English as well as French and Latin.
The Abbasid capital falls in February; the House of Wisdom's books are said to have turned the Tigris black with ink.
The oldest known English song in rounds, celebrating the cuckoo and the coming of summer.
Simon de Montfort's barons defeat and capture Henry III and Prince Edward on 14 May.
In January, Simon de Montfort summons knights and town burgesses as well as lords, a step toward the House of Commons.
On 4 August, Prince Edward kills Simon de Montfort and his body is mutilated.
The Venetian travels to Kublai Khan's court and stays about 17 years.
'Longshanks' conquers Wales, attacks Scotland and reforms English law.
The king commissions Peter Corbet to hunt and kill wolves in several western English counties. Wolves are rare in England by 1300.
Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, the last native Prince of Wales, is killed on 11 December. Edward builds a ring of great castles.
Edward I expels all Jews from England on 18 July. They are not formally readmitted until 1656.
William Wallace and Andrew Moray defeat an English army on 11 September.
The largest surviving medieval world map, with Jerusalem at the centre and monsters at the edges.
Giotto's frescoes in Padua give painted figures real weight and emotion, pointing toward the Renaissance.
Completed around this year, it makes Lincoln the tallest building in the world, beating the Great Pyramid, until it collapses in 1548.
Robert the Bruce defeats Edward II on 23 and 24 June.
Years of endless rain rot the harvests across northern Europe (1315 to 1317). Millions die.
Completed shortly before his death. Written in Tuscan Italian, not Latin.
England and France fight on and off until 1453.
Plague reaches Sicily in October 1347 and England in June 1348. It kills perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population.
Rebels under Wat Tyler march on London in June, burning records and demanding an end to serfdom.
In Falaise, Normandy, a sow that killed a child is tried, dressed in clothes, and publicly executed.
Chaucer begins his stories of pilgrims, written in English when the court still spoke French.
Ming China sends huge fleets across the Indian Ocean as far as East Africa (1405 to 1433).
Henry V's outnumbered army, led by longbowmen, defeats the French on 25 October.
Executed by the English at Rouen on 30 May, aged about 19.
Florence's cathedral dome is finished, built without wooden supports.
Movable metal type makes books cheap. His Bible follows around 1455.
Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II takes the city on 29 May, ending the Byzantine Empire.
First dated printing with movable type
Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz prints letters of indulgence to raise money against the Ottomans. They are the earliest dated documents printed with his type.
Bartolomeu Dias sails around the southern tip of Africa, opening a sea route from Europe to the Indian Ocean.
Lands in the Bahamas on 12 October, starting centuries of colonisation.
Columbus's letter describing the lands he reached is printed in Barcelona, then reprinted in Rome, Paris, Basel and Antwerp within months. Europe's first news bestseller.
Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut, India, on 20 May.
Leonardo keeps working on it for years and never delivers it to the client.
Short printed German news pamphlets called 'Newe Zeytung' (new tidings) report battles, comets, monsters and miracles. 'Zeitung' later becomes the German word for newspaper.
Michelangelo's ceiling is unveiled on 31 October after four years of painting.
Martin Luther publishes his 95 Theses on 31 October. Thanks to print, they spread across Germany in weeks.
In July in Strasbourg, Frau Troffea starts dancing in the street. Within weeks dozens join, some dancing for days.
Magellan's expedition sets out (1519 to 1522). Magellan dies in the Philippines; 18 of about 270 men return.
An epidemic devastates Tenochtitlan. Old World diseases kill a large share of Indigenous Americans over the next century.
Cortes and Indigenous allies capture the Aztec capital on 13 August.
Copernicus publishes his heliocentric model, reportedly seeing the printed book on his deathbed.
Handwritten news sheets called avvisi are sold in Venice, reportedly for a small coin called a gazzetta. That may be where the word 'gazette' comes from.
Gilles Garnier is burned in France after confessing to killing children while in wolf form.
Spain's fleet fails to invade England, scattered by fire ships and storms.
Peter Stumpp is executed in Germany on 31 October after a confession under torture. Pamphlets about the case sell in London.
Elizabeth I charters the English company on 31 December. It later rules much of India.
The Dutch East India Company sells shares to the public in Amsterdam.
A teenager in Gascony claims to be a werewolf. The court decides he is mentally ill and sends him to a monastery instead of executing him.
Guy Fawkes is caught under Parliament with 36 barrels of gunpowder on 5 November.
Johann Carolus of Strasbourg starts printing his weekly 'Relation', recognised as the world's first newspaper. He had been copying the news by hand and wanted to save time.
Willem Janszoon's Duyfken lands on Cape York Peninsula: the first recorded European landing in Australia.
Monteverdi's opera premieres in Mantua on 24 February. One of the first operas still performed.
Galileo sees four moons through his telescope, proof that not everything orbits Earth.
Begins when Protestant nobles throw imperial officials out of a window in Prague. They survive by landing in a dung heap.
'Courante uyt Italien, Duytslandt, &c.' appears in Amsterdam. In 1620 Amsterdam printers also produce the first newspaper in English.
Theophraste Renaudot starts France's first regular newspaper on 30 May, with Cardinal Richelieu's backing. King Louis XIII himself wrote anonymous articles.
In February, Dutch tulip bulb prices collapse after a speculative frenzy.
Descartes publishes his Discourse on the Method.
King Charles I against Parliament. Charles is beheaded in 1649.
On 24 November, Abel Tasman sights the island he calls Van Diemen's Land. In December he reaches New Zealand.
Ends the Thirty Years' War and sets up the modern idea of sovereign states.
'Einkommende Zeitungen' starts publishing in Leipzig, six days a week.
Shah Jahan's tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, built over about 20 years.
The flightless bird of Mauritius is seen for the last widely accepted time.
Kills about 100,000 people, nearly a quarter of the city.
First printed in November as the Oxford Gazette, because the royal court had fled to Oxford from the plague. It is still published today.
Starts in a bakery on Pudding Lane on 2 September and burns for four days.
Laws of motion and universal gravitation.
'Publick Occurrences Both Forreign and Domestick' appears in Boston on 25 September. The colonial government shuts it down after one issue.
An elderly man in Livonia tells a court he is a werewolf who fights witches in hell to save the harvest.
In Massachusetts, 19 people are hanged for witchcraft.
Founded to lend money to the government for war.
Bartolomeo Cristofori builds the first pianos in Florence.
The Daily Courant launches on 11 March: a single sheet of foreign news, with no opinion, so readers could 'make reflections for themselves'.
Shares in the South Sea Company soar and crash. Isaac Newton loses a fortune.
Composed in about 24 days. Premiered in Dublin in April 1742.
On All Saints' Day, 1 November, an earthquake, tsunami and fire destroy Lisbon.
James Watt patents his separate condenser, making steam engines far more efficient.
James Cook's Endeavour lands at Kamay (Botany Bay) on 29 April.
Adopted on 4 July by the Continental Congress.
Adam Smith publishes his founding work of economics on 9 March.
Starts on 1 January as The Daily Universal Register and is renamed The Times in 1788.
British ships arrive at Sydney Cove on 26 January to found a penal colony on Gadigal land.
On 14 July, Parisians storm the royal fortress-prison. The French Revolution begins.
A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
Mary Wollstonecraft argues women deserve education equal to men's.
Edward Jenner inoculates 8-year-old James Phipps with cowpox on 14 May.
Found by French soldiers in Egypt in July. Its three scripts later let Champollion decipher hieroglyphs (1822).
The Sydney Gazette and New South Wales Advertiser appears on 5 March, printed by a convict, George Howe.
On 1 January, after the only successful large-scale slave revolt in history.
On 14 May the Corps of Discovery leaves near St. Louis to cross North America to the Pacific. Sacagawea joins as interpreter and guide.
Premiered in a freezing Vienna theatre on 22 December, in a four-hour concert.
A vat bursts at the Meux brewery on 17 October, sending a wave of beer through the slum of St Giles. Eight people die.
The largest eruption in recorded history, in Indonesia, in April. Tens of thousands die.
In the 'Year Without a Summer' after Tambora, Mary Shelley starts Frankenstein during a ghost-story contest at Lake Geneva.
In late January, Russian (Bellingshausen) and British (Bransfield) expeditions sight the Antarctic continent within days of each other.
The Stockton and Darlington Railway opens on 27 September.
